metadata.title: Digital learning in schools: What does it take beyond digital technology?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected a representative sample of N=410 in-service teachers from German public secondary schools in Bavaria using structured telephone interviews. The paper does not report the use of any student-level or teacher-level survey weights (e.g., sampling/design weights) nor any replicate-weight scheme; therefore, no explicit complex-survey weighting variable is documented. Because the analysis is based on teacher self-report latent-variable measurement and structural equation modeling (SEM) rather than ILSA microdata with PVs, the usual ILSA weight variables are not applicable here. The analytic samples for different SEMs are defined by teachers answering all relevant questions (e.g., N=370 for the frequency-of-use SEM; N=364 for the learning-activity SEM), implying listwise exclusion across model-specific missingness rather than a documented imputation/weighting strategy.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PV) are not applicable because the dependent variables are teacher-reported percentages of digital technology use and teacher-rated frequencies of student learning activities (passive/active/constructive/interactive), not cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA assessment that uses PVs. The paper also does not describe a formal missing-data handling method (e.g., imputation) for the SEMs; instead, it reports that analyses use teachers who answered all relevant questions, but it does not explicitly label the missing-data procedure as listwise deletion or another method. This combination represents a reporting gap for missing-data handling details.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study is teacher-based (not student-based) and uses a representative sample of N=410 in-service teachers from German public secondary schools in Bavaria. Teachers were randomly drawn from administrative districts and school types (Mittelschule, Realschule, Gymnasium) with proportions similar to the Bavarian teacher population. For the SEM predicting frequency of digital technology use during teaching, N=370 teachers answered all relevant questions and were included; for the SEM predicting the four learning-activity outcomes (passive/active/constructive/interactive), N=364 teachers answered all relevant questions and were included. For descriptive comparisons of learning-activity types, N=368 teachers were used for the passive vs constructive/interactive comparisons, and other pairwise comparisons use slightly different Ns (e.g., N=376, N=372, N=381) consistent with model-specific inclusion based on complete responses.

main_findings.target_variable: predicting frequency of digital technology use during teaching
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS the study leveraged Basic digital skills, Technology-related teaching skills, Digital technology in school to predict predicting frequency of digital technology use during teaching, finding that This study uses a representative teacher survey in German public secondary schools in Bavaria (N=410 teachers; telephone interviews, 24 minutes on average, March 6–April 10, 2017) to examine how teachers’ basic digital skills, technology-related teaching skills, and the availability of digital technologies relate to (a) the frequency of digital technology use during teaching and (b) the types of student learning activities teachers foster with digital technology (passive, active, constructive, interactive). The paper reports no machine-learning prediction pipeline; instead, it uses confirmatory factor analysis for latent constructs and structural equation modeling (robust maximum likelihood) to estimate standardized relationships. Teachers reported using digital technology in some way for 43.03% (SD=24.54) of lesson time; passive learning activities were most frequent (13.35%), followed by interactive (10.45%), constructive (10.05%), and active (8.92%). In SEM, basic digital skills were positively associated with frequency of digital technology use (b=0.41) and with passive (b=0.37), active (b=0.29), and interactive (b=0.34) learning activities, while technology-related teaching skills were positively associated with constructive learning activities (b=0.30). Digital technology availability in school was not significantly related to either overall frequency or any learning-activity type. Limitations include reliance on teacher self-report and incomplete documentation of missing-data handling beyond complete-response inclusion. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ILSA/ML because the article is not an empirical large-scale assessment (ILSA) microdata study and does not train or evaluate machine-learning models. The outcomes are teacher-reported percentages and frequencies derived from survey items, and the analysis uses SEM/CFA rather than ML algorithms. Therefore, fields such as main_findings (ML predictive targets) and ml_techniques are intentionally left empty, while the substantive results are summarized in outcome_summary.
